content: 1. Administer ceftriaxone at a dose of 50–100 mg/kg intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV) once daily, in combination with cloxacillin at a dose of 25–50 mg/kg IM or IV four times daily. If there is suspicion of infection beneath an eschar, the eschar should be removed. 2. Ensure adequate pain control, especially before procedures such as dressing changes. For severe pain, administer 1 mg/kg IV every 4 hours. 3. Verify the patient’s tetanus vaccination status. If the patient is not immunized, administer tetanus immune globulin. If the patient is immunized but due for a booster, provide a tetanus toxoid booster. 4. Initiate feeding within the first 24 hours as soon as practical. Children should receive a high-calorie diet with adequate protein, along with vitamin and iron supplements. However, omit iron initially in cases of severe malnutrition. The caloric intake should be five times the normal requirement, and protein intake should be two to three times the normal requirement. 5. To prevent burn contractures, perform passive mobilization of affected areas and splint flexor surfaces to maintain extension. Splints, which can be made from plaster of Paris, should only be worn at night. 6. Begin physiotherapy and rehabilitation early and continue throughout the burn care process. For children admitted for prolonged periods, ensure access to toys and encourage play. 7. Head injuries are a common cause of trauma-related death in children. The primary goal of treatment is to prevent secondary brain damage caused by hypoxia, hypotension, or hypoglycemia. Head injuries may involve skull fractures (closed, open, or depressed) or brain injuries. 8. Concussions are the mildest form of brain injury, characterized by temporary loss of brain function. Contusions involve bruising of the brain, with potential functional impairment lasting hours to weeks. Compression may result from swelling or a growing blood clot (e.g., epidural or subdural hematoma), which may necessitate urgent surgical intervention. Children are more prone to acute brain swelling following severe head injuries. 9. For head trauma, assess the airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) and resuscitate as necessary. Maintain an open airway, ensure adequate breathing, correct shock, and prevent hypotension. If the child is unresponsive to pain or unconscious (P or U on the AVPU scale), seek urgent assistance from an anesthetist to secure the airway. Check for hypoglycemia in young children and correct it as needed. 10. Avoid oral intake in children with suspected skull base fractures. Use an orogastric tube instead of a nasogastric tube. Limit fluid intake to two-thirds of maintenance requirements. Elevate the head of the bed to 30°, but place the child in the recovery position if consciousness is reduced. Diagnose and treat other injuries, and seek urgent review by a pediatric surgeon. 11. Chest injuries in children can be life-threatening and may result from blunt or penetrating trauma. Due to the pliability of the rib cage in children, significant chest injuries can occur without rib fractures. Common injuries include rib fractures, pulmonary contusions, pneumothorax, and hemothorax. All suspected chest injuries require urgent review by a pediatric surgeon. 12. Tension pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space but cannot escape, leading to severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, decreased chest movement, and absent air entry on the affected side. Perform urgent needle decompression followed by insertion of an intercostal drain. Administer oxygen as close to 100% as possible and seek urgent surgical advice. 13. Hemothorax, more common in penetrating chest injuries, involves blood accumulation in the pleural space. Severe hemorrhage can cause hypovolemic shock and respiratory distress. Insert a large chest tube for drainage and seek urgent surgical advice, as ongoing bleeding may require thoracotomy. Administer IV fluids (10–20 mL/kg of normal saline) and transfuse fresh whole blood (20 mL/kg) as soon as possible. Provide oxygen as close to 100% as possible. 14. Pulmonary contusion, a potentially life-threatening condition, involves lung bruising and may progress over 24 hours post-injury. Symptoms include shortness of breath, hypoxemia, and rib fractures. Administer oxygen as close to 100% as possible. 15. Rib fractures may occur at the point of impact and can lead to lung bruising or puncture. In children, ribs typically stabilize within 10 days to 2 weeks, with firm healing and callus formation occurring after 4–6 weeks. 16. Abdominal injuries, common in cases of multiple trauma, may involve blunt or penetrating trauma to various organs. Splenic injuries from blunt trauma and liver injuries from penetrating trauma are particularly common. Assume abdominal injury in any child involved in a serious accident until proven otherwise. Severe abdominal injuries can cause life-threatening internal bleeding. 17. Penetrating abdominal wounds should be assumed to involve intra-abdominal organs. Bowel wall penetration will lead to peritonitis within 1–2 days, necessitating surgical intervention. Be cautious with injuries near the anus, as penetrating rectal injuries can be easily missed. Look for signs of bruising, penetrating trauma, and blood in the urine. Ultrasound, if available, can help detect intra-abdominal bleeding and organ injury. 18. Assess airway patency and breathing, provide oxygen, evaluate circulation, establish IV access, and collect blood for hemoglobin, cross-matching, and amylase activity. Transfuse as necessary and seek urgent surgical advice. 19. Fractures in children heal well if bones are properly aligned. Diagnosis involves identifying pain, swelling, deformity, crepitus, unnatural movement, and loss of function. Fractures may be closed (intact skin) or open (skin wound), with open fractures posing a risk of serious bone infection. 20. For fractures, determine if a fracture is present and identify the affected bone through clinical examination or X-ray. Refer complicated fractures (e.g., displaced, involving growth plates, or open) to a pediatric surgeon. Use posterior splints for upper and lower extremity injuries, ensuring proper alignment and circulation. 21. Supracondylar fractures require urgent reduction if arterial obstruction is present, as indicated by a cool hand, slow capillary refill, and absent radial pulse. Mid-shaft femoral fractures in children under 3 years are treated with a gallows splint, while older children (3–15 years) are treated with skin traction. Monitor circulation and ensure toes remain warm. 22. Wound care aims to stop bleeding, prevent infection, assess underlying damage, and promote healing. Control bleeding with direct pressure. Avoid prolonged use of tourniquets (>10 minutes) to prevent extremity damage. Clean wounds thoroughly with soap, water, or antiseptic, and remove foreign bodies and dead tissue. Administer tetanus prophylaxis as needed. 23. For infected wounds, open the wound, clean it with disinfectant, and pack it lightly with damp sterile gauze. Change dressings daily and administer antibiotics for 5 days or until cellulitis resolves. Use cloxacillin for most wounds to treat potential Staphylococcus aureus infections. 24. Abdominal pain lasting more than 4 hours should be considered a potential emergency. Assess associated symptoms, pain location, and signs of peritonitis, such as tenderness, guarding, rigidity, and absent bowel sounds. Provide nothing orally, insert a nasogastric tube if vomiting or abdominal distension is present, and administer IV fluids. Correct shock with rapid IV boluses of normal saline or Hartmann’s solution. Administer analgesics for severe pain and repeat examinations if the diagnosis is uncertain. Administer antibiotics if peritonitis is suspected and seek urgent surgical review. 25. Appendicitis results from obstruction of the appendix lumen, often caused by fecoliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or gastrointestinal parasites. If untreated, the appendix may rupture, leading to peritonitis and abscess formation.
